Title:
Untying Prefill and Decode Loops in Looped Language Models

Authors:
Yang Hu

Primary category: cs.CL (Computation and Language)
Cross-list: cs.LG (Machine Learning)

Comments:
30 pages, 11 figures. Code, per-item results and a script that recomputes every number: https://github.com/yanghu819/untying-prefill-decode

License: CC BY 4.0

Abstract (plain text):
Looped language models run a block of layers several times for every token and use the same number of loops to read the prompt (prefill) and to generate each answer token (decode). The two phases take very different amounts of time: on Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, prefill is under 0.4% of the time spent on a GSM8K or MATH-500 answer. We ask whether such models should spend more loops on the prompt and fewer on each answer token. We measure where inference time goes on tasks with short and long inputs and outputs, then add LoopBridge, a small adapter with which a decoder with n loops reads the prompt states of any prefill depth m, and vary m from 1 to 16 with one and two decode loops. On Ouro-2.6B with one decode loop, four prefill loops instead of one raise accuracy on four chain-of-thought benchmarks from 31.2 to 41.2 for 16% more time per request, on the same requests and weights; over 11 benchmarks the average rises from 47.2 to 56.8. On most benchmarks the gain stops at two to four prefill loops, also for an adapter trained on prefill depths up to 16. At the same number of decode loops the adapted model beats the original model and models distilled to that depth on the same data, and at one decode loop it also wins at equal measured time (41.2 against 27.0 in about 11 seconds per request). A second decode loop buys more, though: the original model with two loops scores 56.8 in 15.7 seconds, and with two decode loops more prefill loops and distillation reach about the same accuracy in the same time. More prefill loops do not help few-shot MATH or the exact-recall part of HELMET. Code: https://github.com/yanghu819/untying-prefill-decode
